Built For

Every Ophthalmology Practice Across the USA

Ophthalmology billing sits at the intersection of two different payer systems medical insurance for disease management and surgery, and vision insurance for routine care. The code universe in ophthalmology is unique: ophthalmology-specific exam codes (92002-92014) for office visits, E/M codes (99202-99215) for medical eye care when appropriate, and surgical codes spanning cataract extraction through retina, glaucoma, oculoplastics, and cornea surgery.

Retinal injection billing is the highest-volume and highest-value procedure in modern ophthalmology. Anti-VEGF injections for wet AMD, diabetic macular edema, and RVO require both J-code drug billing and 67028 injection procedure billing with prior authorization required by most commercial payers and monthly or quarterly renewal cycles for long-term patients. PMEx manages anti-VEGF authorization as a dedicated workflow, with 48-hour average approval and 45-day advance renewal submission.

The Education

Why Ophthalmology Billing Requires Both Medical

The medical-vision distinction, anti-VEGF billing complexity, and cataract surgery code selection each require specialized expertise. Most general billing teams get at least one wrong.

Ophthalmology billing is the process of coding and submitting insurance claims for both medical eye care and surgical eye procedures using a code set that includes ophthalmology-specific exam codes (92xxx), standard E/M codes (99xxx), and surgical CPT codes for cataract, retina, glaucoma, and oculoplastics procedures.

The most critical coding decision in ophthalmology is the medical vs. routine vision distinction. Medical insurance covers disease management and surgery. Vision insurance covers routine exams and refraction. Coding a medical visit to the wrong payer results in immediate denial. Billing refraction through medical insurance results in denial. Managing both payers simultaneously for patients with both medical eye disease and routine vision needs requires payer-routing expertise most billing teams do not have.

Cataract surgery code selection 66984 for routine vs. 66982 for complex is determined by specific complicating factors in the operative report. Dense or mature cataracts, small pupil, intraoperative complications, and prior eye surgery all qualify for the complex code, which reimburses significantly higher. Most practices bill 66984 by default, leaving the complex code revenue uncaptured even when the operative documentation clearly supports it.

The Highest-Value Coding Split in Eye Care

The Medical vs. Routine Vision Coding Trap

Every ophthalmology visit requires a routing decision: is this medical insurance or vision insurance or both? Medical eye care (disease management, acute conditions, post-surgical care) is billed to medical insurance. Routine vision care (refraction, contact lens fitting, routine exams) is billed to vision plans. When a patient has both active eye disease and routine vision needs at the same visit, billing must be split correctly between the two payers.

Billing a routine vision exam to medical insurance results in denial routine exams are not covered. Billing a medical eye disease visit to a vision plan results in significantly lower reimbursement than the medical payer would provide and the practice forfeits the medical insurance revenue entirely. PMEx applies a payer-routing check to every ophthalmology encounter identifying the correct code set, the correct payer, and the correct patient cost-sharing for each service category.

When a patient presents with diabetic retinopathy requiring OCT imaging, examination, and refraction, PMEx routes the medical care to medical insurance with 92014 or 99214, routes refraction (92015) to the vision plan, and ensures both payers are billed correctly on the same day of service.

Medical Eye Care Billed to Vision Plan

Systematic across all diabetic eye disease patients. $143 per visit lost without generating a denial because the vision plan pays the wrong amount rather than denying the claim.

PMEx routes every encounter to the correct payer based on diagnosis and service type. Medical eye disease visits go to medical insurance. Routine vision care goes to vision plans. Split-day billing managed when both payers apply to the same visit.

Anti-VEGF Auth Lapse

Retinal Injection Without Active Authorization

Bevacizumab injection administered to wet AMD patient. Prior authorization expired 8 days prior. Commercial payer denies the $1,800 injection and $185 procedure claim retroactively. Drug already administered, no recovery.

PMEx tracks anti-VEGF authorization renewal cycles for every retinal patient submitting renewals 45 days before expiration. Every injection has active confirmed authorization before the patient is placed in the treatment chair.

Cataract Code Error

Complex Cataract Billed as Routine

Dense cataract with posterior capsule fibrosis documented in operative report qualifying for 66982. Billed as 66984 (routine). $640 per case reimbursement differential missed. Across 200 cataract cases per year, that is $128,000 annually from a single miscoding pattern.

PMEx reviews every cataract operative report for complex qualifying factors dense or mature cataract, small pupil, prior vitrectomy, intraoperative complications, zonular instability. Complex code applied when documented. Routine code applied when criteria are absent. Zero default-to-routine coding.

OCT Billing Error

Retinal OCT TC and Professional Component Not Split

OCT equipment owned by the practice. OCT interpretation performed by the ophthalmologist. Global code billed instead of separate technical (92134-TC) and professional (92134-26) components. Revenue impact depends on facility arrangement up to $85 per OCT study miscoded.

PMEx determines the correct TC/PC billing structure for each ophthalmology practice based on equipment ownership and professional interpretation arrangement. Correct component billing applied from the first OCT claim submitted.

Premium IOL Disclosure

Medicare ABN Not Documented for Premium IOL

Medicare patient elects toric IOL upgrade. Medicare covers the standard monofocal IOL; patient pays upgrade difference. ABN (Advanced Beneficiary Notice) not documented before procedure. Medicare denies the upgrade billing due to missing required patient financial disclosure documentation.

PMEx manages the complete premium IOL billing workflow confirming ABN documentation before surgery scheduling, billing the covered monofocal IOL component through Medicare, and invoicing the patient separately for the upgrade premium with correct documentation.

BOTOX Medical

Medical BOTOX for Blepharospasm Coded Incorrectly

Blepharospasm treatment with onabotulinumtoxinA (J0585) billed without prior authorization or with wrong diagnosis codes. Commercial payer denies for missing auth or incorrect diagnosis. $400 to $800 per blepharospasm treatment session uncollected.

PMEx manages medical BOTOX billing for ophthalmology prior authorization for blepharospasm treatment, correct J0585 units based on injected dose, correct diagnosis codes (G24.5, G51.3), and billing to medical insurance rather than cosmetic self-pay.
